tagline: A mountain microstate with two princes
overview:
Tucked high in the Pyrenees between France and Spain, Andorra is one of the smallest countries in the world. At 468 square kilometers it would fit inside New York City with room to spare. The capital, Andorra la Vella, sits about 1,000 meters above sea level, making it the highest capital city in Europe. Around 80,000 people live here, and most of them are not Andorran citizens but residents from Spain, Portugal, and France who came for work.

Andorra has an unusual government. It is a co-principality, meaning it has two heads of state at once: the President of France and the Catholic Bishop of Urgell in Spain. In practice a parliament called the General Council makes the laws. The official language is Catalan, the only country where that is true. Andorra earns its living from visitors, about eight million a year, who come to ski in winter, hike in summer, and shop in its tax-free stores. It uses the euro but is not a member of the European Union.
landAndNature: Every part of Andorra is mountainous. Three steep valleys, carved by the Valira rivers, meet at the capital, and the peaks around them top 2,900 meters at Coma Pedrosa, the highest point. Winters bring heavy snow that feeds the Grandvalira and Pal-Arinsal ski areas, while summers are mild and sunny. Dozens of small glacial lakes, called estanys, sit in high rocky basins above forests of pine and fir. Chamois, a nimble mountain goat-antelope, leap across cliffs, marmots whistle from the meadows, and golden eagles and huge bearded vultures circle overhead. The Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley, a quiet glacial valley with no road at all, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
peopleAndCulture: Catalan is the official language, but Spanish, Portuguese, and French are heard everywhere, and many children grow up speaking three or four languages. Traditional dishes reflect hard mountain winters: trinxat is a hearty mash of potato, cabbage, and bacon, and escudella is a thick stew of meat, beans, and pasta served at winter festivals. On the night of the summer solstice, young people carry blazing torches down the mountainsides in the falles, a fire festival recognized by UNESCO. Tiny Romanesque stone churches with slender bell towers, some nearly a thousand years old, dot the villages. Skiing is the national sport, and Andorra sends a small team to every Olympic Games.
history: Legend says the emperor Charlemagne granted Andorra its first charter in the 800s, and the national anthem still praises him. Real records begin in 1278, when a dispute between a French count and the Bishop of Urgell was settled by agreeing to share power over the valleys. That arrangement, with the count's rights passing over time to the French head of state, has lasted more than 700 years, making Andorra one of the oldest continuous states in Europe. For centuries its people farmed, raised sheep, and grew tobacco in isolation. Andorra stayed neutral in both world wars. In 1993 it adopted its first written constitution, giving real power to an elected parliament, and joined the United Nations the same year.
funFacts: Andorra has no airport and no army; France and Spain are responsible for its defense.
The country has one of the longest life expectancies in the world, often placed in the top five.
Andorra la Vella, at over 1,000 meters, is the highest capital city in Europe.
With about eight million visitors a year, tourists outnumber residents roughly a hundred to one.
Andorra's tax-free shops make it a giant open-air mall, and its main avenue is lined with electronics and perfume stores.
